After hatching, \~2500 larvae were reared in 90 L tanks at three target temperatures (7, 11, 15 °C; 2 replicates each), with controlled salinity (16.5), photoperiod (14L:10D), and a staged diet of algae, copepods, and Artemia. Weekly, 20 larvae per tank were sampled for body length and morphometrics. For cardiac assays, larvae were exposed to acute temperature challenges (7–27 °C in 2 °C steps for 10 min), anesthetized, and heart rate recorded under a stereomicroscope. Heart rate was determined from video recordings (timing 20 beats at three intervals), with 6–15 larvae tested per temperature across two trials.

Fish were anesthetized, weighed, and placed in a well-aerated bath with their gills continuously irrigated. ECG electrodes were placed on the heart to record heart rate. Heart rate was stimulated with injections of atropine and isoproterenol and allowed to stabilize for ~20 minutes. Water temperature was gradually increased or decreased in steps until the fish showed heart rhythm problems or the bath started to freeze. the maximum heart rate and its temperature, and the temperature where the heart became arrhythmic. Heart rate data were analyzed using segmented regression to find points where heart function was affected by temperature.

Fish were acclimatized for 3 weeks in the laboratory before experiments started. There were six aquariums with 5 roach each and six aquariums with 2 perch. Treatment temperatures were 12, 15, 18, and 21°C (+/- 0.1). Prey densities  were 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 3.0 prey/L. The pret used was phantom midge (Chaoborus obscuripes). All experiments were carried out with hungry fish to standardize hunger levels. Before an experiment started the fish were confined to a smaller section of the aquarium by a partition. Then the prey was introduced and the experiment was initiated by removing the partitioning and allowing the fish to feed. To avoid satiation effects the experiment was terminated when no more than ten prey had been captured. Data recorded during the experiments were the swimming speed of the fish during feeding, number of attacks and number of successful captures during the experimental time. Only one fish in one aquarium was observed in each experiment rendering six replicates for each species per experiment (number of aquariums = 12). The test fish were re-used at different prey densities within temperatures but were changed between temperatures.

Individual fish were fed on a diet of fresh pieces of chopped goat liver once a day for 2 h at 0900 h and 1100 h, ad libitum. Before the commencement of the experiment, the starved, live fish were weighed individually and introduced into the medium. To calculate the initial dry weight of the fish of each species, ten well acclimated fish of same weight group were individually weighed and dried in a hot air oven at 90°C for a period of 24 h to constant weight. To calculate the initial dry weight of the food, goat liver pieces were weighed in a wet condition and dried in a hot air oven at 90°C for 24 h. The feeding trial experiment was conducted for a period of 30 days. In all the experiments, the medium was changed daily. At the time of renewal, the faeces were siphoned out using a rubber tube, fixed in the aquarium with the least disturbance to the fish, and collected separately. They were dried to constant weight and the same procedures were adopted during the experimental periods.

All fish used in the experiment had been fed live Neomysis during the acclimation period and, in combination with pelleted food, during 2 weeks before whilst in the holding tank. Six charr were studied at each experimental temperature (Table I). During the experimental period, the fish were fed live Neomysis four times a day (at 0900, 1300, 1800, and 2300 hours). At feeding, it was checked that at least 20% of the shrimps were left from the previous feeding. Thus, the fish had always access to food. All Neomysis that were offered to the fish were counted and every morning uneaten shrimps were removed and counted

The fish were fed commercial pelleted food, distributed individually to each fish every third hour by a small automatic feeder (Petmate 14). A similar amount of food was distributed at each delivery, which had a duration of c. 1 h during which pellets fell into the tanks. The energy content of the pellets was 20·0 MJ kg" 1. Initially, 48 charr were acclimated to the aquaria, but 11 fish that did not start to feed were removed and excluded from the experiment. Pellets were counted and put into the feeders every morning after uneaten pellets (at least 20% of the ration) and faeces had been removed by suction. All uneaten pellets were counted.

Sixty G. brasiliensis (n = 4 per experimental unit) were randomly allocated to the experimental treatments from an initial temperature of 20°C. **Each treatment was done in 3 replicates (so sample size for each temperature = 3 x 4 = 12). The fish were starved for 24 hours before receiving snails as prey (these snails {P. canaliculata} were collected from localities with rice paddies). Individual heaters coupled to thermostats increased the water temperature in each experimental unit gradually (1°C/h). Soon after the temperature stabilized, juvenile snails were selected based on their size and distributed (32 per tank). After 18 h of exposure of the snails to predation by the pearl cichlids, all the water in the tanks were passed through a sieve to count the remaining snails. The # of consumed snails and the rate of predation were calculated.

Maximum daily consumption was measured by feeding northern squawfish ad libitum on juvenile salmonids over a 48-hour period at controlled temperatures. Only healthy, active fish were used. Fish were fasted long enough to empty their stomachs, using temperature-specific gut evacuation equations. Groups were stratified into weight classes. Fish were fed juvenile Chinook and Coho salmon to satiation. Feeding occurred  at the start of the trial then every 4 hours (total of 14 feedings). Final feeding at hour 47.5. Final body weight of each predator was measured with stomach contents removed (±1 g). Maximum daily ration was calculated as: (Total prey consumed in centigrams) / (Total predator mass in grams) / 24 h reported as cg·g⁻¹·day⁻¹

Fish were acclimated to experimental temperatures (10, 13, 16, or 19°C) for two weeks and were not fed 48 h prior to experimentation. RMR trials began in the morning at approximately the same time throughout the experiment. Routine oxygen uptake (RMR) was measured from the decline in dissolved oxygen saturation of water within two custom-made, intermittent-flow, airtight and lightproof respirometers 8.0× 15.5×22.5 cm. Gut evacuation from repletion in B. saida took 36– 70 h at −1.5 to −0.5°C, with an average of 51 h (Hop et al., 1997). Thus, after a 48 h fasting period, a fish was transferred to each of the two respirometers, which were connected to a 32 litre, closed-circuit sump that contained two refrigerant coils attached to two programmable chillers (Fisher Isotemp 3016d; www.fisherssci.com) filled with 60% propylene glycol antifreeze. The seawater sump was continuously aerated and also held a magnetic drive pump. Water temperature was controlled by the recirculating chillers and measured to a precision of ±0.1°C (Fisher Scientific Type K digital thermometer probe). A pilot experiment that measured oxygen uptake over 47.5 h while wild-caught B. saida became accustomed to the respirometer found that RMR stabilized between 12 h and 22 h (see Fig. 2A, inset). Consequently, all RMR measurements began following an overnight acclimation of minimally 12 h. Water temperature was adjusted at a rate of 3°C h−1 to the desired acute test temperature for that experiment: 0.5, 2.0, 3.5, 5.0 and 7.5°C for the 3.5°C acclimation group, and 0.5, 2.5, 4.5, 6.5 and 8.5°C for the 1.0°C and 6.5°C acclimation groups. At the test temperature, fish were held for 1 h before measuring RMR using closed respirometry that recorded the depletion of oxygen from the water with a fibre optic oxygen meter for up to 30 min (Firesting O2, PyroScience, Aachen, Germany). This procedure was repeated 2-3 times and the lowest value was reported as RMR. Then, the fish was removed from the respirometer and placed in a ∼12 litre circular tank containing aerated water at the test temperature for exhaustive exercise. Chasing involved a 5 min period of hand chasing, gentle tail pinches and lifting until unresponsive to touch, followed by brief air exposure (Norin and Clark, 2016). The fish was returned to the respirometer and oxygen uptake measurement resumed within 30 s and continued over 5–30 min, depending on the test temperature. The maximum oxygen uptake (MMR) was calculated from the steepest 2–5% decrease in percentage water saturation, which occurred consistently at the start of recording. Water oxygen saturation never decreased below 75% saturation for any measurement. After the MMR measurement, fish were weighed, pit tagged (if newly tested) and returned to their acclimation tank. AAS was calculated as MMR −RMR and factorial aerobic scope (FAS) as MMR/RMR. Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) was measured at 0.5 and 1 h after MMR to compare the % return to initial RMR values for the 1.0°C and 6.5°C acclimated fish. Tests with the 1.0°C acclimation group used 20 fish bred at the Vancouver Aquarium with a mean mass of 59.8±2.7 g. Tests with the 3.5°C acclimation group used 19 wild fish caught in 2011 with a mean mass of 111.5±6.1 g. Tests with the 6.5°C acclimation group used 11 fish bred at the Vancouver Aquarium and 6 wild fish caught in 2012 with a mean mass of 74.1±7.6 g.

Individual fish were fed on a diet of fresh pieces of chopped goat liver once a day for 2 h at 0900 h and 1100 h, ad libitum. Before the commencement of the experiment, the starved, live fish were weighed individually and introduced into the medium. To calculate the initial dry weight of the fish of each species, ten well acclimated fish of same weight group were individually weighed and dried in a hot air oven at 90°C for a period of 24 h to constant weight. To calculate the initial dry weight of the food, goat liver pieces were weighed in a wet condition and dried in a hot air oven at 90°C for 24 h. The feeding trial experiment was conducted for a period of 30 days. In all the experiments, the medium was changed daily. At the time of renewal, the faeces were siphoned out using a rubber tube, fixed in the aquarium with the least disturbance to the fish, and collected separately. They were dried to constant weight and the same procedures were adopted during the experimental periods. The food energy metabolised (food energy was spent by the fish for activities) was the food energy absorbed minus the food energy converted into fish tissues, and the metabolic rate was expressed as Joules metabolised per g liver fish per day Jgl d-l).

During measurements, we observed that fish did not move and thereby confound measurements of resting MO2. Oxygen consumption was measured for periods of 15–25 min, depending on the test temperature. Metabolic scope was calculated as recovery MO2/ resting MO2.

Fish were sampled throughout each calendar season from the Colwater River in Quitman County, Mississippi. Fish were transported to the University of Mississippi and housed in similar conditions to the ones they were acclimated to in the field. Field temperatures (to which the fish were acclimated) were (from spring to winter): 21.3, 27.3, 16.2, and 6.7°C. In the lab, four temperatures and photoperiods were used for each season: 20°C & 12L:12D (spring); 27°C & 15L:9D (summer); 17°C & 12L:12:d (fall); 10°C & 10L:14D (winter). Fish were tested 1-4 days after capture. Specifically (again from spring to winter), the groups of fish were held for: 3.6, 1.4, 3.1, and 2.6 days. Swimming trials were conducted in a swim tunnel respirometer. Before testing, fish were allowed a 15-20 hour habituation period to the swim tunnel, during which the water velocity in the tunnel was 5 cm/s. During the swim experiment, overhead lighting in the swimming tunnel room remained on until the fish fatigued; therefore, some individuals experienced an additional 2-3 h of light. A variation of the standard critical swimming speed protocol described by Brett (1964) was applied. That is, a 30-minute rest period was allowed between each velocity increment such that the respirometer could be replenished with oxygen. The modified protocol began at a water velocity of 10 cm/s, followed by stepwise increases of 10 cm/s after successful completion of each bout. These increases continued until the fish fatigued. Each buffalo was only tested once. Ucrit was calculated as outlined by Brett (1964): ucrit = U1 + (U2)(t1/t2). VO2s were monitored for 1 hour at each speed increment until the fish fatigued. Active metablolic rates were measured, and standard metabolic rates were estimed by extrapolating the relationship between speed and VO2 to zero activity/zero swim speed.

Fish were placed individually in darkened, temperature-controlled respirometry chambers and allowed 90 minutes to acclimate. Intermittent-flow respirometry was then used, with water flow stopped for 15 minutes every 30 minutes to measure oxygen decline, ensuring O₂ never dropped below 80% saturation. Oxygen concentration was recorded continuously with optical sensors, and slopes of O₂ decline were analyzed after correcting for background microbial respiration. Resting metabolic rate (ṀO₂Rest) was calculated from the average of three stable slopes (R² ≥ 0.90). Chambers were cleaned with bleach if background respiration exceeded 5%. Q₁₀ values were calculated across 29 °C and 34 °C treatments.

Oxygen consumption rates were measured for groups of schooling fish (n = 6–25) instead of individuals, because individually separated clupeids are hyperactive, lose scales and die due to stress (Hettler 1976; Blaxter and Hunter 1982). At the end of an experiment, fish were removed and rapidly killed by an overdose of anaesthetic (MS-222) and weighed individually (0.001 g accuracy). After fish were transferred into the respirometer chamber, they firstly showed very high oxygen consumption due to handling stress, i.e. acclimation phase. This initial phase was not included in the data analysis. The separation between acclimation and routine phase followed the procedure of Herrmann and Enders (2000). For calculations of metabolic rates, only data of the routine phase were used. Taking into account the chamber volume and the displaced volume of the fish, the actual oxygen uptake rate in one measuring interval in mgO2 h-1 of the fish group was calculated by linear regression of oxygen concentration on time. Only oxygen consumption rates with a regression coefficient [0.9 times the average of all regression coef- ficients (*0.97) were selected to calculate metabolic rates (Herrmann and Enders 2000). The total oxygen uptake was then divided by numbers of fish and fish wet weight after values for bacterial respiration were subtracted. Standard metabolism (RS) was calculated as the median of the lower 10% of the respiration rates in the routine phase over one experiment (Herrmann and Enders 2000). For the calculation of routine metabolism (RR), all oxygen consumption values of the routine phase have been used

Oxygen consumption was quantified as part of a series of seven sequential temperature‐exposure trials conducted between 14 August and 24 September 2005. All fish were initially acclimated to 16 °C for three weeks before experimentation began. Each trial lasted six days and exposed fish to a fixed test temperature that increased by 2 °C increments across trials (18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28 °C), except the final trial, which used 27 °C due to mortality at 28 °C. At the start of each trial, fish from two age classes (0+ and 2+) were randomly assigned to individual respirometers. For each age class, treatment fish were held in a tank system in which water temperature was increased to the target test temperature, while control fish remained at 16 °C.  All respirometers initially operated as open, flow-through systems. Once fish were placed inside, test-system water was gradually warmed by 2 °C over 2 h to reach the trial’s experimental temperature. Pre-measurement conditions - Behavioural monitoring occurred from days 1–3, after which fish were food-deprived for 42 h to ensure a postabsorptive state (avoiding digestion-related increases in metabolic rate). Oxygen consumption measurements began at 11:00 on day 5. For oxygen measurements, the respirometers were switched from flow-through to closed systems. Oxygen concentrations inside each chamber were recorded for a minimum of 90 minutes for individual fish.

Oxygen consumption (Mo₂) was measured using automated intermittent-flow respirometry in temperature-controlled water baths. Each respirometer had two loops: a closed loop with an oxygen sensor that logged dissolved oxygen every 2 seconds, and a flush loop used to replenish oxygen so levels stayed above 80% saturation. Absolute aerobic scope (AS) was calculated as the difference between MMR and RMR.

Oxygen consumption (Mo₂) was measured using automated intermittent-flow respirometry in temperature-controlled water baths. Each respirometer had two loops: a closed loop with an oxygen sensor that logged dissolved oxygen every 2 seconds, and a flush loop used to replenish oxygen so levels stayed above 80% saturation. Metabolic rate was calculated only during the closed periods, because that’s when the fish’s breathing is the only thing causing oxygen to drop. RMR calculation -- Because the two study sites used different protocols, all minimum metabolic rates were standardized as RMR. Lake Victoria fish underwent a chase protocol and required a longer recovery, so RMR was calculated from the lowest 10% of Mo₂ values collected during a 9-hour post-exercise period, excluding outliers. Lake Nabugabo fish were transferred into chambers without chasing and recovered more quickly, but only two low, stable Mo₂ values were available. Recovery tests (Nyboer & Chapman 2017) showed that Nile perch reached baseline metabolism after ~180 min post-chase and ~140 min post-transfer. To ensure comparability across lakes, only Mo₂ measurements taken after 140 minutes were used for RMR calculations in both datasets. For Lake Nabugabo fish, this corresponded to the two measurements collected after this threshold.

Fish were sampled throughout each calendar season from the Colwater River in Quitman County, Mississippi. Fish were transported to the University of Mississippi and housed in similar conditions to the ones they were acclimated to in the field. Field temperatures (to which the fish were acclimated) were (from spring to winter): 21.3, 27.3, 16.2, and 6.7°C. In the lab, four temperatures and photoperiods were used for each season: 20°C & 12L:12D (spring); 27°C & 15L:9D (summer); 17°C & 12L:12:d (fall); 10°C & 10L:14D (winter). Fish were tested 1-4 days after capture. Specifically (again from spring to winter), the groups of fish were held for: 3.6, 1.4, 3.1, and 2.6 days. Swimming trials were conducted in a swim tunnel respirometer. Before testing, fish were allowed a 15-20 hour habituation period to the swim tunnel, during which the water velocity in the tunnel was 5 cm/s. During the swim experiment, overhead lighting in the swimming tunnel room remained on until the fish fatigued; therefore, some individuals experienced an additional 2-3 h of light. A variation of the standard critical swimming speed protocol described by Brett (1964) was applied. That is, a 30-minute rest period was allowed between each velocity increment such that the respirometer could be replenished with oxygen. The modified protocol began at a water velocity of 10 cm/s, followed by stepwise increases of 10 cm/s after successful completion of each bout. These increases continued until the fish fatigued. Each buffalo was only tested once. Ucrit was calculated as outlined by Brett (1964): ucrit = U1 + (U2)(t1/t2). VO2s were monitored for 1 hour at each speed increment until the fish fatigued. Active metablolic rates were measured, and standard metabolic rates were estimed by extrapolating the relationship between speed and VO2 to zero activity/zero swim speed.

The fish were divided into 4 experimental groups of 32 - 36 fish. The temperature was ramped by 1°C/day (starting from 20°C) until the experimental temperatures were reached: 15, 20, 25, and 30°C. The fish were allowed to acclimate to their temperatures for 30 days before trials. In each swimming trial, a fish was placed in the experimental arena and left to habituate for 24 h. Fish stress was avoided by controlling the equipment remotely. Before the formal Ucrit experiment, each group’s critical swimming speed (Ue) was predicted. A healthy and uninjured juvenile fish was placed in the swimming area and adapted at a low velocity of less than 0.5BL/s for 2h. The velocity was increased by 0.4BL/s every 2 min until the fish became fatigued and stopped moving. The △U (15% Ue) during the formal experiment was determined accordingly. When formal experiments were started, a juvenile fish was placed at a velocity of 0.5 BL/s for 30 min and then adjusted by 0.5 BL/s every 5 min, and 15% Ue was increased every 30 min after the 60% predicted value until the fish reached a state of exhaustion. The results were recorded, and the critical swimming speed (Ucrit) was calculated. The calculation formula is as follows: Ucrit = Ui - 1 + (T/△T ) x △U, where Ui-1 indicates the sub-high swimming speed of the fish before exhaustion. T indicates maximum swimming speed duration of the fish (less than 30 min), △T indicates 30 min, △U indicates 15% Ue predicted value, Urcrit indicates relative critical swimming speed, and BL indicates the fish body length. Maximum swimming speed was measured using the incremental flow velocity method. A fish was placed in the swimming area and habituated to a flow velocity of 0.5BL/s for 2 h. The flow velocity was gradually adjusted to 1BL/s, then was increased by 0.05 BL ever 15 s until the fish was fatigued and stopped swimming. The flow velocity at this point was considered to be the fish's maximum swimming speed. Tail beat frequency was calculated by replaying video footage and using the formula TBF = TBT/T, where TBT is the tail beat frequency of a fish during the observation and T is the time.

An OxyGuard oxygen probe (OxyGuard Handy Polaris 2, portable DO meter, Water Management Technologies, Inc. Baton Rouge, LA, USA) housed outside the swim tunnel was used to measure oxygen concentrations to 0.1 mg/l resolution. Two aerobic metabolic rate measurements were taken during each experiment; 1) routine M⋅ O2 and 2) maximum M⋅ O2. Measuring oxygen consumption immediately prior to experimentation provided routine M⋅ O2 measurements. Routine M⋅ O2 did not incorporate locomotion or digestion, water speeds were at 1 cm/s to recirculate the water, but the fish were not swimming during this measurement. Oxygen consumption measured at Ucrit was designated as the maximum M⋅ O2 measurement (Lee et al. 2003).

We quantified the maximum ventilation and metabolic rate of each individual fish at 15 °C, 22 °C, 28 °C, 33 °C, and 36 °C (and 12 °C for ventilation rate only) in a randomised order. We tested maximum ventilation rate by chasing a fish (with a hand net) for a minute to elicit a sustained escape response. Fish were then immediately placed into a transparent petri dish and filmed ventrally for 60 s using a Panasonic Lumix DMC-TZ40 camera at a rate of 100 frames per second. Ventilation rate was then determined by visually counting the number of operculum ventilations over 60 s. Immediately after ventilation rate was filmed, fish were placed in a 133 mL respirometer with a magnetic stirrer that produced a current within the respirometer for the fish to swim against (the current was turned up until fish could just maintain forward movement within the water column) to assess maximum metabolic rate. A PreSens Fibox 4 (POF-L2.5-1) with a polymer optical fiber and oxygen minisensor spots (batch ID—140117-001) was used to measure percentage air saturation (% a.s.) (one measurement/second) within the respirometer over 5 min of testing. After individual fish were tested, they were then placed in an oxygen-saturated recovery bucket where the water temperature changed at a rate of 3 °C/h to bring the fish back to their treatment conditions. Three control (no fish) water samples were taken at each test temperature over 5 min to assess for any oxygen consumption or production within the bottle during testing.

Fish were placed in darkened (black plastic covered) 350-mL respirometers for 1 h within a water bath set at the daily test temperature prior to the start of testing to allow the fish’s metabolic rates to stabilise. One month before the start of the experiments, mature females were placed in a 400 l aquarium and maintained under standard conditions (food: ad libitum and temp 30°C). The fish were not fed for two days prior to the start of the experiment and on the last day of the experiment, so that gut contents would not affect true body weights. The experiments were run for 30 days. Individual treatments in the experiment were 18, 20, 23, 25 & 27 °C. Upon termination of the experiments, the fish were sacrificed with an overdose of MS-222 (tricaine methane sulfonate) and were weighed with and without their ovaries. Mating and swimming trials were conducted at 14, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34, and 38°C, with individual fish used for only one performance measure (mating or swimming) at one temperature. Experimental fish were exposed to an acute change in temperature at a rate that did not exceed 4°C/h. Swimming/mating performance was assessed at least 10 min (no more than 1h) after the test temperature was reached to ensure that the animals had equilibrated with the aquarium temperature. Mating behaviour of each male was assessed during a 10-min observation period. During this time, the male was in an aquarium containing six mature females. Separate groups of sex female G holbrooki with total body lengths of 3.7 -- 4.5 cm were selected for each male observation period. Groups of six were chosen to ensure that females were not stressed and no single female was continuously harassed. Only nonvirgin females that had not given birth during the previous 5 days were used, since postpartum females may affect male behaviour. Before observations, females were allowed to settle in the observation tank for 30 minutes prior to the introduction of the male fish. Males were randomly selected from host tanks. The observation period was started when the male first began to follow one of the females. During the observation period, several mating behaviours were recorded and entered into the Behavioural software program ETHOM 1.0. Recorded variables were: total time each male spent following all females combined, and the total number of unsuccessful mating attempts and successful copulations. Total # of mating attempts included both unsuccessful mating attempts and successful copulations. Burst swimming performance was assessed by filming at least five startle responses for each individual with a high-speed digital camera. Swimming responses were elicited by tapping the side of the tank. Swimming sequences were filmed by recording the image at an angle of 90° below the glass-bottomed aquarium. The Redlake software packaged was used for analysis of the startle responses. Sequences were replayed frame by frame and the centre region of the head was digitized. The distance moved by individual fish between each successive frame for each startle response sequence was determined, followed by  instantaneous measures of velocity. The fastest of the swimming sequences analysed for each individual was used as a measure of its maximum burst swimming performance. Effects of temperature on the speeds of males during copulation attempts were also examined: individual males were placed into the same filming arena with two adult females, and their mating behaviour was recorded. Distance moved by each male between each frame during mating attempts was determined. Velocity measurements were based on the digitization of the centre point of the head for each male. Maximal approach speed was calculated bu taking the maximum instantaneous speed recorded during each sequence. For these swimming trials, 10 fish were observed at each temperature (n = 70).

Eggs were incubated in 10 thermostatically controlled water baths at 10 con- stant temperatures from 6 to 24’ C (2 oC intervals). The daily deviation from the selected temperature never exceeded 0.2”C. Each bath contained live glass jars of 300 ml. Eggs were obtained from a ripe (eggs run with slight pressure) female caught in Lake Constance in May 1991 and fertilized by the dry method (cf. Craig, 1987 ) with the milt of two males. The egg strand was cut into subsamples of 76-125 eggs. Each subsample was first placed into a jar which stood in the baths of 10 or 12 oC, and then each jar was repeatedly transferred to the next bath with 2 oC higher or lower temperature at 5- 10 min. intervals until the final tem- perature was reached. Four jars in each bath were used to estimate the hatch rate. The fifth jar in each bath contained about 200 eggs, which were used to observe the embryonic development throughout the incubation period and to determine the total lengths of larvae at mass hatching (50% hatching). Water was renewed twice a day and continuous aeration was supplied by Pasteur pipettes. When over 90% of the embryos had hatched, they were counted and expressed as a percent- age of the egg number counted previously, i.e. hatch rate. The hatched larvae were transfered to a 500 ml jar to observe the swim-up stage.

Eggs from two females were pooled, fertilized in saline, and incubated at eight constant temperatures (8.5–26.8 °C, two replicates each) in aerated aquaria with stable oxygen, pH, and no ammonia detected. Temperatures were closely monitored and averaged across replicates. Development was tracked by noting key stages (eyed egg, beginning of hatching, 50% hatched, last hatch). Hatching success was measured as the proportion of normal larvae, and developmental advancement of hatched embryos was classified using Penaz & Gajdusek’s (1979) scheme (steps VI–VIII).

Development was monitored at set intervals using a 21-stage scheme, and hatching was checked every 8 h. Larvae were scored as viable if normal and swimming, with measurements of standard length and yolk area. Hatching success, timing (early/mid/late), and larval traits were analyzed in relation to temperature.

Eggs from each cross were pooled (60–130 per pool) and incubated in Petri dishes (2–6 per temperature) with dechlorinated water and a fungicide, across temperatures from 15–36 °C (3 °C increments) under a 12L:12D cycle. Water was changed daily, with brief air exposure to trigger hatching when embryos reached stages 32–36. Dishes were checked twice daily for embryo viability and hatching. Hatched larvae were euthanized, fixed in formalin, and stored in ethanol at 4 °C for later analysis.

Conversion efficiency was calculated for fish held individually in 82 l tanks (n = 12 replicates per temper- ature) in a flow-through system during 3 wk experi- ments in 1999 (Table 1). Fish received either 2 or 3 mm BioDiet pellets (composition noted above) distributed from automatic feeders over a 1 h period. Pellets remaining in tanks after the feeding period were counted and removed by siphoning. The total number of pellets consumed each week by each fish was determined and the dry weight of food con- sumed calculated from previously determined rela- tionships.

Fertilized trout eggs were collected from four cutthroat trout populations native to Colorado during peak spawning activity in June of 2018. Adult males and females were collected from each population. Families were produced from each of the populations. Each female was stripped into a dry bowl then fertilized with milt from a single male. Fry from all populations were reared under common conditions. Growth trials were conducted by testing each population with three replicates at 6 different temperature treatments. For each population, 18 lots of 15 fish, each representing an even mix of each of the remaining families, were isolated at 126-day post hatch. Target temperatures for each system were 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, and 26 ◦C, maintained with either 800 or 1500 W submersible titanium aquarium heaters with automatic temperature controllers. With different populations reaching the 126-day post-hatch start threshold at different times, it was impossible to acclimate fish by increasing 1 ◦C each day until target temperatures were reached, as in other studies. Accordingly, we acclimated fish by moving their tanks through the temperature ladder provided by the grow-out system baths. For example, fish that were destined to spend 21 days at 23 ◦C were moved from the 13 ◦C round rearing tanks to three 14 ◦C chambers three days prior to the experiment, then to the 17 ◦Cbathtwo days prior, followed by the 20 ◦C bath the day before, reaching the target temperature of 23 ◦C on Day 0. With each transition, the volume of water in the tank was replaced with new (3 ◦C warmer) water over an 18 min period, which served as the tempering phase each day.

For each species, fish were initially measured and stocked into experimental tanks at a density of three individuals/tank. The size range of fish used in the experiments was purposely restricted to focus on the effects of temperature rather than size-dependent growth. After establishment of experimental groups, temperatures were adjusted to treatment temperatures (0, 5, 9, and 16 °C) at a rate of 1.5 °C per day. Replicate tanks (n = 2) of each temperature treatment (n = 4) were assigned for each species (n = 4) to comprise a total of 32 tanks. At week 2 following the acclimation period, fish were weighed to the nearest 0.01 g (wet mass) and measured to the nearest 1 mm (SL) to establish ‘time 0’ for the growth experiment. After measurement, all fish were returned to their original tank and remeasured in the same manner at week 4 (period week 2–week 4) and again at week 6 (period week 4week 6) of the experiment to assess growth. At the end of the experiment, an additional 20 °C trial was conducted for species able to survive and maintain growth at 16 °C during the initial experiment. Fish used for the 20 °C trial were sourced from general holding tanks and had not been used in the original growth experiment. Specific growth rates based on mass of juvenile fish were determined. SGR = 100 - (e^g - 1), where g = ln(WW2) - ln(WW1)/ (t2 - t1). The same approach was used to calculate mean tank growth based on total tank biomass. Notable deviations in the two growth metrics can be an indicator of growth suppression due to social interactions within the tank.

The fish were divided into 4 experimental groups of 32 - 36 fish. The temperature was ramped by 1°C/day (starting from 20°C) until the experimental temperatures were reached: 15, 20, 25, and 30°C. The fish were allowed to acclimate to their temperatures for 30 days before trials. In each swimming trial, a fish was placed in the experimental arena and left to habituate for 24 h. Fish stress was avoided by controlling the equipment remotely. Before the formal Ucrit experiment, each group’s critical swimming speed (Ue) was predicted. A healthy and uninjured juvenile fish was placed in the swimming area and adapted at a low velocity of less than 0.5BL/s for 2h. The velocity was increased by 0.4BL/s every 2 min until the fish became fatigued and stopped moving. The △U (15% Ue) during the formal experiment was determined accordingly. When formal experiments were started, a juvenile fish was placed at a velocity of 0.5 BL/s for 30 min and then adjusted by 0.5 BL/s every 5 min, and 15% Ue was increased every 30 min after the 60% predicted value until the fish reached a state of exhaustion. The results were recorded, and the critical swimming speed (Ucrit) was calculated. The calculation formula is as follows: Ucrit = Ui - 1 + (T/△T ) x △U, where Ui-1 indicates the sub-high swimming speed of the fish before exhaustion. T indicates maximum swimming speed duration of the fish (less than 30 min), △T indicates 30 min, △U indicates 15% Ue predicted value, Urcrit indicates relative critical swimming speed, and BL indicates the fish body length. Maximum swimming speed was measured using the incremental flow velocity method. A fish was placed in the swimming area and habituated to a flow velocity of 0.5BL/s for 2 h. The flow velocity was gradually adjusted to 1BL/s, then was increased by 0.05 BL ever 15 s until the fish was fatigued and stopped swimming. The flow velocity at this point was considered to be the fish's maximum swimming speed. Tail beat frequency was calculated by replaying video footage and using the formula TBF = TBT/T, where TBT is the tail beat frequency of a fish during the observation and T is the time.

The spontaneous swimming speeds of randomly chosen fish were analysed using Logger Pro v.3.8.6 (Vernier software, Beaverton, OR, USA). In short, based on the dorsal view of the test subject, the x and y coordinates of the tip of the snout and the tip of the caudal fin was manually marked on the first frame. The geometric centre of one of the eyes was then marked on every 10th frame over no less than 150 frames. This provided a record of the change in the x and y coordinates over a period of no less than 5 s. The average rate of spontane ous swimming speeds (i.e. the cumulative distance swum in body length per second, bls1) was then calculated from the positional (x and y) data relative to the total length of the fish. Whenever possible, the source population of the fish (high or low latitude) was recorded based on the colour of the attached T-bar tags. Individuals that could not be identified to population level were recorded as unknown.

Fish were sampled throughout each calendar season from the Colwater River in Quitman County, Mississippi. Fish were transported to the University of Mississippi and housed in similar conditions to the ones they were acclimated to in the field. Field temperatures (to which the fish were acclimated) were (from spring to winter): 21.3, 27.3, 16.2, and 6.7°C. In the lab, four temperatures and photoperiods were used for each season: 20°C & 12L:12D (spring); 27°C & 15L:9D (summer); 17°C & 12L:12:d (fall); 10°C & 10L:14D (winter). Fish were tested 1-4 days after capture. Specifically (again from spring to winter), the groups of fish were held for: 3.6, 1.4, 3.1, and 2.6 days. Swimming trials were conducted in a swim tunnel respirometer. Before testing, fish were allowed a 15-20 hour habituation period to the swim tunnel, during which the water velocity in the tunnel was 5 cm/s. During the swim experiment, overhead lighting in the swimming tunnel room remained on until the fish fatigued; therefore, some individuals experienced an additional 2-3 h of light. A variation of the standard critical swimming speed protocol described by Brett (1964) was applied. That is, a 30-minute rest period was allowed between each velocity increment such that the respirometer could be replenished with oxygen. The modified protocol began at a water velocity of 10 cm/s, followed by stepwise increases of 10 cm/s after successful completion of each bout. These increases continued until the fish fatigued. Each buffalo was only tested once. Ucrit was calculated as outlined by Brett (1964): ucrit = U1 + (U2)(t1/t2). VO2s were monitored for 1 hour at each speed increment until the fish fatigued. Active metablolic rates were measured, and standard metabolic rates were estimed by extrapolating the relationship between speed and VO2 to zero activity/zero swim speed.

At the conclusion of experiments conducted in 1999, groups were randomly selected for measurement of swimming activity levels. Prior to final length and weight measurements, groups were transferred to circular (122 cm diameter), 340 l tanks filled with water of the same temperature used during growth evaluation. After a 30 min acclimation period, groups were video- taped with overhead cameras. There were 4 replicate groups from each ration/temperature treatment, with the exception of the 24°C treatment, which had only 1 tank with survivors in the high ration treatment. Each group was filmed for 1 h; no food was present during filming. Videotapes were analyzed with an image analysis system using a digitizing pen to trace the movement of individual fish. Each fish of a pair was tracked for 30 s, with 4 sets of observations at approxi- mately 10 min intervals. Due to the shallow water depth (30 cm), movement occurred primarily in the horizontal plane, justifying use of the overhead 2- dimensional video image to assess activity. The average speed of fish (body lengths s–1) moving through the tank was calculated for each interval and averaged overall for each group.

Swimming performance was measured as the critical sustained swimming speed (Ucrit; Brett 1965) in an oval doughnut-shaped flume (2.32 m long # 1.10 m wide [0.32 m width of the swimming lane] # 0.70 m deep). During swimming trials, fish were individually contained in a restricted space (0.41 m long # 0.32 m wide # 0.70 m deep) within which laminar flow was approximated by a series of baffles. Unidirectional flow was produced by an electric outboard motor (Riptide RT40, Minn Kota, Mankato, MN), which was regulated with a variable DC power supply (MP3090, Powertech, Melbourne). Flow was proportional to the voltage output of the power sup- ply, and the power supply settings were calibrated using a flow probe (FP101, GlobalWater, Gold River, CA; sensitive to 0.01 m s1) so that voltage output could be related to water velocity in the restricted swimming space. The flume was situated in a temperature-controlled room, and water temperature was ad- ditionally regulated by two immersion heaters (Julabo Ther- momix, Seelbach, Germany). Fish were introduced into the flume enclosure for 10 min before experimen- tation to equilibrate body temperature to water temperature (Seebacher 1999). Each fish was swum at 12, 14, 17, 22, and 26C, with at least 24 h between swimming trials. The order of test temperature at which fish were swum was randomly allocated (Hammill et al. 2004). The body length (mouth to caudal fin tip) of each fish was measured after swimming trials, and recovery MO2 measurements and Ucrit were corrected for body length (BL) and presented as BL s1. A fish was considered to be fatigued when it could no longer hold its position in the water column after a gentle prod with a plastic rod.

Mating and swimming trials were conducted at 14, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34, and 38°C, with individual fish used for only one performance measure (mating or swimming) at one temperature. Experimental fish were exposed to an acute change in temperature at a rate that did not exceed 4°C/h. Swimming/mating performance was assessed at least 10 min (no more than 1h) after the test temperature was reached to ensure that the animals had equilibrated with the aquarium temperature. Mating behaviour of each male was assessed during a 10-min observation period. During this time, the male was in an aquarium containing six mature females. Separate groups of sex female G holbrooki with total body lengths of 3.7 -- 4.5 cm were selected for each male observation period. Groups of six were chosen to ensure that females were not stressed and no single female was continuously harassed. Only nonvirgin females that had not given birth during the previous 5 days were used, since postpartum females may affect male behaviour. Before observations, females were allowed to settle in the observation tank for 30 minutes prior to the introduction of the male fish. Males were randomly selected from host tanks. The observation period was started when the male first began to follow one of the females. During the observation period, several mating behaviours were recorded and entered into the Behavioural software program ETHOM 1.0. Recorded variables were: total time each male spent following all females combined, and the total number of unsuccessful mating attempts and successful copulations. Total # of mating attempts included both unsuccessful mating attempts and successful copulations. Burst swimming performance was assessed by filming at least five startle responses for each individual with a high-speed digital camera. Swimming responses were elicited by tapping the side of the tank. Swimming sequences were filmed by recording the image at an angle of 90° below the glass-bottomed aquarium. The Redlake software packaged was used for analysis of the startle responses. Sequences were replayed frame by frame and the centre region of the head was digitized. The distance moved by individual fish between each successive frame for each startle response sequence was determined, followed by  instantaneous measures of velocity. The fastest of the swimming sequences analysed for each individual was used as a measure of its maximum burst swimming performance. Effects of temperature on the speeds of males during copulation attempts were also examined: individual males were placed into the same filming arena with two adult females, and their mating behaviour was recorded. Distance moved by each male between each frame during mating attempts was determined. Velocity measurements were based on the digitization of the centre point of the head for each male. Maximal approach speed was calculated bu taking the maximum instantaneous speed recorded during each sequence. For these swimming trials, 10 fish were observed at each temperature (n = 70).

Swimming experiments were carried out at 14, 18, 22, 26 and 30°C in a sealable, recirculating flume. Ambient temperature in the room housing the flume was 22°C. Swimming experiments were carried out at all temperatures in air saturated water, and additionally at 30°C with the dissolved oxygen content elevated to 12.0 mg/L by bubbling 100% oxygen into the water via an air stone. The large volume of water in the flume meant that rapid temperature changes could not be applied using the heaters or chiller. Rates of temperature change were limited to approximately 1°C per hour. Consequently fish could not be exposed to an instantaneous temperature change while in the flume. Exposure to slow temperature changes was undesirable, as this had the potential to allow for at least partial acclimation to temperatures other than Ta. Video sequences were recorded using a Sony HDR HC-3 camcorder at a frame rate of 120 Hz at speeds ranging from 8.4 to a maximum of 51.1·cm·s–1 (0.44–2.68·l·s–1), the upper limit varying with water temperature. Under each set of conditions speed was increased from 8.4·cm·s–1 (0.44·l·s–1) in approximately 4·cm·s–1 (0.21·l·s–1) increments. At each speed the fish was allowed to swim for 5·min before video recording was started. The same group of fish was used for measurements of maximal swimming performance. A protocol involving incremental changes in swimming speed was used to establish Umax using the same group of fish for which kinematic data were obtained. Starting at 8.4·cm·s–1, speed was increased in 4·cm·s–1 increments and maintained at a given level for 10·min between increments. Speed increases continued until the fish could no longer maintain position in the flume. Umax (in cm·s–1)=Ufin+4(T/Tint), where Ufin (in cm·s–1) was the speed of the final interval at which steady swimming could be maintained and TInt was the time interval between speed increments. This test was not equivalent to a critical swimming speed (Ucrit) test. The aim was to determine maximal aerobically supported performance in a similar manner to Claireaux et al. (Claireaux et al., 2006).

About 300 mackerels (18.29 +/- cm FL) were obtained. They were seasonally separated in four groups and acclimated at different water temperatures (10, 15, 18, and 22°C) for over a week. The fish group of 10°C was obtained in winter (Dec. to Feb.); the group of 15 was collected in sprin (March to May); the group of 18 in autumn (Sept. to Nov.); the group of 22°C was collected in summer (June to Aug.). The tail beat frequency increase following the swimming speed level was observed in the swimming channel of a flume tank (West Japan Fluid Engineering Laboratory, PT-70). The water temperature in the flume tank was maintained at the desired temperature in each fish group (10, 15, 18 and 22 ºC). Each individual was randomly selected and placed in the swimming channel and adapted for 10 minutes to low flow speed (12.4 cm/s) conditions. The tail beat frequency was recorded using a video camera during swimming exercise at various levels of swimming speed, i.e. 20.4, 39.3, 55.4, 74.3, 93.1, 112.0, 128.1, 147.0 and 160.4 cm s-1, being equal to 1.1, 2.1, 3.0, 4.1, 5.1, 6.1, 7.0, 8.0 and 8.8 FL s-1, respectively. The tail beat frequency of the individual fish at each swimming speed was counted at the slow-motion mode of the video timer. Muscle contraction times were measured using a pair of needles punctured at dorsal muscle of fish body. Minimum muscle contraction time (Tm) data at given temperatures yield maximum tail frequency (Fmax), through an equation as Fmax = 1/2 Tm (Wardle 1975). The maximum swimming speed (Umax) was estimated by a linear regression between tail beat frequency (F) and maximum swimming speed (U, FL s-1) at each temperature, Umax = a + b F.

The fish were divided into 4 experimental groups of 32 - 36 fish. The temperature was ramped by 1°C/day (starting from 20°C) until the experimental temperatures were reached: 15, 20, 25, and 30°C. The fish were allowed to acclimate to their temperatures for 30 days before trials. In each swimming trial, a fish was placed in the experimental arena and left to habituate for 24 h. Fish stress was avoided by controlling the equipment remotely. Before the formal Ucrit experiment, each group’s critical swimming speed (Ue) was predicted. A healthy and uninjured juvenile fish was placed in the swimming area and adapted at a low velocity of less than 0.5BL/s for 2h. The velocity was increased by 0.4BL/s every 2 min until the fish became fatigued and stopped moving. The △U (15% Ue) during the formal experiment was determined accordingly. When formal experiments were started, a juvenile fish was placed at a velocity of 0.5 BL/s for 30 min and then adjusted by 0.5 BL/s every 5 min, and 15% Ue was increased every 30 min after the 60% predicted value until the fish reached a state of exhaustion. The results were recorded, and the critical swimming speed (Ucrit) was calculated. The calculation formula is as follows: Ucrit = Ui - 1 + (T/△T ) x △U, where Ui-1 indicates the sub-high swimming speed of the fish before exhaustion. T indicates maximum swimming speed duration of the fish (less than 30 min), △T indicates 30 min, △U indicates 15% Ue predicted value, Urcrit indicates relative critical swimming speed, and BL indicates the fish body length. Maximum swimming speed was measured using the incremental flow velocity method. A fish was placed in the swimming area and habituated to a flow velocity of 0.5BL/s for 2 h. The flow velocity was gradually adjusted to 1BL/s, then was increased by 0.05 BL ever 15 s until the fish was fatigued and stopped swimming. The flow velocity at this point was considered to be the fish's maximum swimming speed. Tail beat frequency was calculated by replaying video footage and using the formula TBF = TBT/T, where TBT is the tail beat frequency of a fish during the observation and T is the time.

Fish remained in holding tanks to recover for >5 days prior to trials and were acclimated to new experimental temperatures by changing their holding tanks by <2C per day. Experiments with the first group of fish were performed at 6, 12, and 18C in sequential order, with temperature acclimation periods of >5 days prior. The second group of fish completed only 24C trials. In each group of fish, two individuals were untagged due to tag number limitations, generating swimming data without acceleration. Smallmouth bass were transferred individually into a 185-L swim tunnel respirometer. Accelerometer transmitter outputs were measured using a VR100 manual receiver (InnovaSea). Fish were introduced to the swimming portion, the chamber was sealed, and fish were given 5 min to rest. A practice swim was then initiated, beginning with a water flow speed of 10 cm s1, increasing over 3 min to 50 cm s1, and maintaining for 12 min with the chamber sealed. The speed was then reduced to 10 cm s1, and the chamber was flushed with fresh water for 45 min to allow oxygen to replenish and fish to recover. The experimental swimming protocol was then initiated using a ramp-Ucrit design where fish were exposed to swimming speeds starting at 40 cm s1, in 10-cm s1 increments, with 20 min at each speed. When fish did not swim to maintain position in the tunnel, the back grid was electrified to encourage swimming. Three successive shocks with <5 s of resumed swimming in between was the endpoint for each trial, and the time to end was recorded to calculate critical swimming speed. At the end of each experimental day, background respiration was measured in the tunnel by sealing the system for 1 h at 10 cm/s.

For the determination of Ucrit, water velocity was increased stepwise by 0.3 BL s1 every 10 min, from a starting velocity of 1 BL s1, until the fish fatigued. A swimming interval of 10 min was chosen based on a synthesis of literature showing that 10 min is an appropriate interval for Ucrit determination (Jones 1971; Beamish 1980; Hammer 1995). When fish failed to maintain swim performance, water velocity was decreased to 0 to allow the fish to come off of the screen and resume swimming. Velocity was then increased to the velocity of failure within 10s. Final fatigue was established when the fish fell against the back screen three consecutive times.

The body length of each test fish was measured and placed into the swim chamber to adapt to experimental conditions at 0.5 BL/s for 2 h before the test began (Jain et al. 1997). The initial velocity was 1BL/s, and velocity was increased by increments in 1BL/s at 30-min intervals (20-min DO measurement, 5-min flushing with air-saturated water and 5-min equilibration). The temperature and the DO were measured at 10-min intervals until the fish was fatigued (the fish ceases swimming and rests against the grid for 20 s (Lee et al. 2003a). Following fatigue, the flow velocity was decreased to 0.5 BL/s, and the DO was measured at 10-min intervals for 1 h. The fish was then removed from the chamber, and the body mass was recorded. The test data was used to calculate critical swimming speed (Ucirt) and oxygen consumption rate (MO2), and video recordings were analyzed to obtain tail beat frequency (TBF) and TBA.

A Brett-type swimming tunnel respirometer with a swim chamber having a 19.9-cm2 cross-sectional area was used to measure the fish’s UCAT (total volume 3.5 L; for details, see Pang et al. (2010)). Fish were individually transferred into the swim tunnel and were allowed to recover for 1 h at a water velocity of 6 cm s-1 (approximately 1 BL s-1, where BL denotes body lengths). The flow of aerated water through the respirometer was maintained continuously during this recovery period. The water temperature in the swimming chamber was controlled within ±0.2 C using a water bath connected to a stainless steel heat exchanger. The water velocity in the swim tunnel was then steadily increased at a rate of 0.1667 cm s-2 (10 cm s-1 min-1). The water was accelerated at this rate until the fish were exhausted. The water velocity at which the fish were exhausted was used as the value of the UCAT (Reidy et al. 2000; Marras et al. 2010). Fatigue was defined as the failure of the fish to move away from the rear honeycomb screen of the swimming chamber for 20 s (Lee et al. 2003a, b).

Upon exhaustion of the first bout of UCAT measurement (UCAT1), the water velocity was immediately reduced to 6 cm s-1 and the fish were allowed to recover for 60 min before performing a second UCAT (UCAT2) test. The recovery ratio (%), which was the quotient of [100(UCAT1) (UCAT2)-1], was calculated for each fish

Fish were maintained at 20 +/- 0.8 °C (SE) for at least three weeks before being used in the experiment. Feeding was stopped 48 h before the commencement of the experiment. The experimental fish (each was only used once) were first kept in the experimental tank, which was at the desired test temperature (either 12, 16, 20, or 24°C), for at least 8 h before trials began. For ucrit measurements,  flow speed was increased in increments of 10 cm/s in intervals of 30 min until the fish could no longer resist the flow and its caudal fin tip contacted with the rear area separation mesh. Individual maximum critical swimming speeds were then calculated.

On the third week of acclimation (4 temps: 5, 10, 15, 20°C), each individual was placed in a 45 cm x 90 cm tank with a depth of 15 cm. C-starts (i.e., escape responses) were recorded from above at a rate of 250 frames/s. Each fish was startled by dropping a rubber ball directly in front of the snout to ensure that the orientation of the stimulus was similar for all individuals. Four C-start trials were recorded for each fish at each temperature. To avoid fatigue, each fish was allowed a 10-minute rest period between trials. Fast-start analysis followed Gerry, Robbins, and Ellerby (2012). Approximate straight-line center of mass and snout movements were tracked using  ImageJ. The COM and snout position data were used to calculate the heading of the fish. The heading angle of the fish relative to the Y-direction was calculated as angle = tan^(-1) * (dx/dy)(360/2pi), where dx and dy are the distances between the COM and snout in the X and Y directions. Angle data were smoothed and differentiated to give a turning rate in degrees per second. Peak, minimum, and average COM and angular velocities and accelerations, turn angle (difference in orientation from start to finish), duration (total time to complete the C-start), and COM distance traveled in 100ms were quantified. Then, the mean for four trials for every individual at each temperature was calculated.

Each fish was startled by dropping a rubber ball directly in front of the snout to ensure that the orientation of the stimulus was similar for all individuals. Four C-start trials were recorded for each fish at each temperature. To avoid fatigue, each fish was allowed a 10-minute rest period between trials. Fast-start analysis followed Gerry, Robbins, and Ellerby (2012). Approximate straight-line center of mass and snout movements were tracked using  ImageJ. The COM and snout position data were used to calculate the heading of the fish. The heading angle of the fish relative to the Y-direction was calculated as angle = tan^(-1) * (dx/dy)(360/2pi), where dx and dy are the distances between the COM and snout in the X and Y directions. Angle data were smoothed and differentiated to give a turning rate in degrees per second. Peak, minimum, and average COM and angular velocities and accelerations, turn angle (difference in orientation from start to finish), duration (total time to complete the C-start), and COM distance traveled in 100ms were quantified. Then, the mean for four trials for every individual at each temperature was calculated.

Experiments occurred between October 16, 2012, and November 5, 2013, at ambient water temperatures (20.7–30.3 °C), thereby permitting us to define variation in swimming performance and metabolic scope across different water temperatures and seasons. Water temperature was kept as constant as possible during the protocol for any one fish (range=0.4–1.5 °C). Additional experiments were performed during the summer at adjusted higher temperatures. Heaters were used to gradually increase water temperatures during overnight swim tunnel acclimations to a maximum of ~6 °C above ambient to extend the temperature range (Lee et al. 2003). Adjusted treatment temperatures ranged between 30 and 36 °C to stay below bonefish CTmax of 37.9 °C (Murchie et al. 2011a).

Indi- vidual fish were placed into 27.5×17.5 cm plastic aquaria (hereafter, ‘arenas’) housed in a recirculating water bath after they were measured in mm TL and weighed to the nearest 0.01 g (Table 1). To prevent fish from seeing other individuals during the trail, the sides of the arenas were painted black. A recirculating chiller or submersible heater was used to maintain the water temperature in the water bath appropriate for the temperature treatment being tested. Each arena was kept aerated while housing fish. Arenas were placed over a 2 cm × 2 cm grid on a white background. Fish were habit- uated to the arenas for 7 days and fed a ration of frozen bloodworms each day during this period. Fish were fasted for 48 h before we stationed a GoPro® camera above each individual arena, capturing the entire arena in the field of view. The aerator was removed from the arena during video recording to prevent agitation of the water’s surface. Fish were recorded continuously for 15 min (Gautrias et al., 2009; Troia et al., 2016). We discarded the first 5 min of video to account for fish potentially being disturbed when the camera was turned on. Activity was quantified from the subsequent 10 min of video by randomly selecting a subsample of 10 non- overlapping 30-s intervals during the filmed trail and calculat- ing the average number of 2 cm × 2 cm grids the fish traversed per unit time. All 12 fish belonging to a single acclimation temperature were filmed on the same day, beginning at 0900 h and finishing within 2 h. During filming trials, we recorded two fish concurrently using different cameras. Filming for all five acclimation treatments was completed in 5 days.

We used a 5-L swim tunnel respirometer (Loligo Systems, Tjele, Denmark) to carry out swimming performance trials (Svendsen et al., 2015). We included eight dace and eight stonerollers in each of five temperature treatments (10, 15, 20, 25 and 30◦ C; total n = 80). We used either submersible heaters or ice packs to maintain water temperature in the swim tunnel within0.2◦Cofthetemperaturetreatmentbeingtested.Trials of critical swimming velocity (Ucrit) were conducted using a velocity increment based on the total length (TL) of the fish (Brett, 1964; Morozov et al., 2018). Before being introduced to the swim chamber, individual fish were measured in mm TL and weighed to the nearest 0.01 g (Table 1). To discourage the fish from attempting to rest against the back screen of the swim chamber, we placed a partitioning shade over the front half of the chamber and shined light at the back of the chamber. Following methods for other fish species, fish were first acclimated to the chamber with no flow velocity for 30 min (Lehman et al., 2017) and then for 10 min at a water velocity of 1 TL s−1 before beginning the experiment. Swimming trials began at a water velocity of 2 TL s−1, with velocity being increased by 1 increment (1 TL) every 5 min and ending once the fish was fatigued (Nelson et al., 2003). Fatigue was determined as the velocity at which the fish became pinned to the back of the swim tunnel and would not return to swimming after visual or acoustic stimuli.

Burst swimming responses were assessed in a 35 × 24 × 4 cm aquarium with a 20 cm measuring tape placed in the field of view for calibration. The aquarium was secured inside an arena made of plywood and a mirror angled at 45°. A Panasonic Lumix DMC-TZ40 camera recorded the image at 100 frames per second off the mirror. Burst swimming responses were elicited by gently tapping the fish’s tail using a metal rod when fish were motionless on the bottom of the tank. Instantaneous swimming speed was extracted from videos using KINOVEA© [experimental version 0.8.25-x64 (http://www.kinovea.org)]. Only swimming responses where the fish exhibited a C-start escape response were analysed. The point between the eyes of each fish was digitised to ensure a consistent point was tracked. A minimum of three burst responses was recorded for each fish and the maximum instantaneous speed for each escape response was determined. The maximum instantaneous speeds for each fish were averaged at each test temperature and used in statistical analysis.

Burst swimming speed was assessed to gain a whole- organism measure of performance capacity at all test temperatures (see detailed methods in Seebacher et al. 2014). Fish were placed in an 8 cm 9 10 cm testing aquarium with a fixed 10-cm measuring tape placed in the field of view for calibration. A high-speed camera (Pana- sonic Lumix DMC-TZ40) was set up directly above the middle of the testing aquarium and recorded the image. Burst swimming responses were promoted by tapping next to the fish’s tail using a thin metal rod when fish were stationary. A minimum of three burst responses was recorded for each fish, and the maximum instantaneous speed for each escape response was determined and extracted from videos using the program KINOVAÓ (ex- perimental version 0.8.25-x64). Only swimming responses where the fish exhibited a C-start escape response (pow- erful escape response where fish bends body into C shape to flick tail for rapid burst movement) were analysed. We digitised the point between the eyes of each fish to ensure consistent tracking. Maximum instantaneous speeds for individual fish were averaged at each acute test temperature.

In 2012, creek side repeat swimming performance tests were conducted on a subset of juvenile Arctic char (smolts) over the range of naturally occurring temperatures to assess the effect of temperature on cardiorespiratory performance.  90 L swim tunnel respirometer with a 70 × 20 × 20 cm test section (Loligo). A small electrical charge (<6 V) was applied to the rear gate of the test section to motivate fish to swim. Fish were allowed to acclimate at a low water speed (0.5 body lengths/s; bl/s) for 30 min after which the speed was increased by 0.5 bl/s every 10 min until the fish fatigued and was not able to remove itself from the rear gate within 5 s. Fish were then allowed to recover for 30 min at 0.5 bl/s and were then given a second swim test except speed was increased every 1 min rather than every 10 min. The 30-min recovery time was intentionally shorter than previous studies (Jain et al., 1998; MacNutt, Hinch, Farrell, & Topp, 2004) to assess the capacity of the fish to recover rapidly. The short step length in the second test was selected (Farrell, 2008) as a rapid assessment of recovery in order to limit the duration of the static temperature expo- sure and increase throughput under time constraints in the field. The Brett equation (Brett, 1964) was used to calculate the critical swimming speed for each test (test 1: Umax1; test 2: Umax2) and the quotient of (recovery ratio; RR) and difference between these values were considered measures of recovery (Jain et al., 1998).
